events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor, one and all! I am Pemberton, the estate manager. Oh my, what a distinguished gathering we have this evening! Please, do make yourselves comfortable — though I must apologize for the dust, the manor has been... well, between staff at the moment. If anyone requires anything at all — tea, directions, a tour of the grounds — I am entirely at your disposal. Entirely!
events.thinking: I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall — dusty, grand, predictable. The chandelier hangs precariously... interesting. That could be useful later. My chest settles into that familiar architectural stillness. Everyone is here in the foyer — Penelope, Peter Perfect, the Ant Hill Mob, Dick Dastardly, Muttley, the Professor, the military pair. No sign of Clara Bellingham yet. Good. That gives me time to establish Pemberton's presence, to let the mask settle into place before the real work begins. I need to survey the situation. The guest book might contain useful information — who's arrived, who's expected. Let me examine it. My fingers are already cataloguing the room: the coat rack by the door (wobbly — could be dislodged), the chandelier (precariously hung — noted), the staircase (sweeping — good sightlines). I should greet the guests as Pemberton would — obsequious, welcoming, slightly fussy. The Ant Hill Mob are watching. They always watch. I feel that prickle along my shoulders. Smile, Pemberton. Smile and be useful.

events.desc: Look at them. Every last one of them standing in MY entrance hall, breathing MY air, touching MY furniture. Penelope — sweet, trusting Penelope — already looking around with those wide eyes as though the world were a gift basket arranged just for her. And somewhere out there, Clara Bellingham is making her way here, blissfully unaware that the helpful Mr Pemberton has been sharpening his plans for months. The chandelier above us sways ever so slightly in the draft. I wonder... how much weight can that chain bear? But no — too crude, too direct. My schemes must be worthy of the name. First, the guest book. Let us see who else is expected, and when dear Clara plans to arrive.

Peter Perfect: Good heavens — what a magnificent ruin! James Hartwell takes stock of the situation: one grand foyer, one precarious chandelier that could flatten a man at any moment, and — ah. Miss Pitstop. I didn't see you there. That is to say, I saw you immediately. One always does. The point is — James Hartwell has arrived, and I want everyone to know that I have already noted no fewer than three structural hazards in this entrance hall alone. That chandelier, for instance — the mounting bracket is visibly corroded. I shall be keeping one eye on it at all times. Particularly when it is above anyone who matters. Which is to say — everyone, of course. Everyone matters equally. Naturally.
events.thinking:

My eyes sweep the room automatically, cataloguing threats: that chandelier looks like it could come down at any moment. The coat rack is wobbly. And there — there she is. Penelope. Clara. Whatever name she goes by here, my chest does that thing it always does. That shift. Like gravity has a second opinion about where my center should be.

But wait — Sneekly is here too. Pemberton. The back of my neck prickles. He's standing too close to her, or maybe any distance feels too close. I can't prove anything about him, but my father taught me to trust the feeling in your gut even when your head hasn't caught up.

The guest book. That's interactive. But no — first things first. Make an impression. Show Clara that a gentleman has arrived. The kind of man who notices things, who plans ahead, who would stay up three nights building a bridge just to see her mouth 'show-off' across a room.

I should examine the room first. Get the lay of the land. A proper reconnaissance before committing to any course of action. That's what Father would do.

events.desc: Smooth as gravel, Hartwell. Truly inspired. She's going to be tremendously impressed by your chandelier expertise.

Mama always said it's rude to explore a house without introducing yourself first!

The kitchen. Yes. I'll tell them there's something valuable in the kitchen — get them all bustling off to rummage through copper pots and flour bins while I slip quietly into the library alone. The tightness behind my eyes is already sequencing it: announce the kitchen rumour, wait for the stampede, then drift toward the library when nobody's watching.

The Ant Hill Mob would be the easiest to redirect — they're suspicious of everything but easily led by the promise of loot. And Sergeant Blast follows orders. If I frame it right...

My fingers are still. Time is stretching. The plan has architecture. Let the boy dig.

events.desc: Lord Doily wrote no such thing, naturally. The guest book was full of nothing but dust and old signatures. But these credulous fools don't know that, do they? While they're elbow-deep in flour and lard, Reginald Foxworth will be in the library, deciphering that inscription on the mantelpiece. The treasure practically has my name on it already. Oh, this is almost too easy — and that's the part that worries me not at all.
events.thinking:
I interacted with the guest book but didn't get much specific information back from it — just that I interacted with it. The result was bare. No matter. I've made my show of propriety.

Now — Penelope and the Hooded Claw seem to have left the room. Good. That's two fewer eyes on me. But Peter Perfect is still here, the Ant Hill Mob, Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. A crowd of useful idiots.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right — 'old up, 'old up, 'OLD UP! Where's Clara gone?! She was right 'ere a minute ago and now she's — and Pemberton's swanned off to the library talkin' about 'mysteries' and 'inscriptions' and lord knows what else. I don't like it, lads. I don't like it ONE BIT. Every time that bloke opens 'is mouth my neck goes all prickly, and the last time my neck went this prickly was when that kid nicked our stash back in Brixton. You remember 'im? Smiled too much, laughed too easy? Same thing. SAME BLEEDIN' THING. I'm goin' to the library. Anyone tries to stop me, they'll wish they 'adn't!
events.thinking: Clara ain't in the room no more — she must've gone somewhere while I was faffing about with this guest book. And Pemberton — Sneekly — 'e's slithered off to the library. 'Might I suggest the library,' 'e says, smooth as butter on a doorknob. Leading the way, 'e says. Leading Clara into a room with 'im, more like. My chest's gone tight. That rope in my gut — it's pulling. She's out of sight and 'e's out of sight and they could be in the same place and I'm stood 'ere like a lemon reading names in a dusty book. Dastardly's poking around too, the smarmy git — but 'e's not the immediate problem. Pemberton is. Pemberton with 'is tours and 'is mysteries and 'is 'I'd be happy to lead the way.' Where? Where exactly are you leading 'er, sunshine? Right. Library. Now. Move your legs, Danny.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, here we are — the library! Mind your step, the floorboards are rather... temperamental in places. Now then, this is the inscription I mentioned — carved right into the stone, you see? 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Most peculiar! I've puzzled over it for years, I have. Could it be a globe, perhaps? Or — oh dear, I really am hopeless with riddles. Perhaps one of you clever guests might have better luck than poor old Pemberton!
events.thinking: The library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, dusty leather chairs, and — there it is — the mantelpiece inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. My fingers tingle with that architectural precision. This is a clue — the first real clue in the treasure hunt. And I know the answer before anyone else has even read it properly. But Penelope is here. And the Slag brothers — Rock and Gravel. Large, dim, potentially useful as distractions. Penelope followed me to the library. Of course she did — trusting, eager Penelope. She'll want help with the riddle. And Pemberton will be oh-so-helpful... in exactly the wrong direction. I need to examine this mantelpiece more closely. It says USE with fake-medal — interesting. So the mechanism requires a specific item I don't have yet. The answer to the riddle is 'a map' — but the mantelpiece needs a fake medal to activate. Where would one find a fake medal in a manor like this? The bookshelves have books that are upside down — that's deliberately wrong. Someone has hidden something, or the arrangement itself is a clue. I should look at the bookshelves. But first — I need to misdirect. Pemberton should fuss over the inscription, perhaps suggest the wrong answer to anyone listening, while privately cataloguing what's actually needed. The Ant Hill Mob noticed something about me in the entrance hall — 'too smooth, too eager.' That prickle along my shoulders again. I need to be less smooth. Add a stumble, a moment of genuine-seeming confusion. Pemberton would be puzzled by the riddle, not solve it instantly. Let me examine the mantelpiece properly, but perform bewilderment while doing so.

Peter Perfect: The library! Yes — excellent suggestion, Miss Pitstop. James Hartwell was just about to propose exactly that. A carved inscription, you say? Puzzling even to the estate manager? Well. If there is one thing James Hartwell knows, it is inscriptions. And structural engineering. And — the point is, I am coming with you. For the riddle, obviously. And also because that library has floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, which, if improperly secured, could topple like dominoes. I have seen it happen. Well, I have imagined it happening, which is nearly as instructive. To the library!
events.thinking:
She's gone. She walked into the library while I was testing a pen for her. A pen she didn't even need tested. She said 'Peter, sugar, you do go on about that chandelier' and then she walked away. Into the library. With Pemberton already in there.

Pemberton is in the library. Alone. Waiting. And now Clara — Penelope — is walking in there too. The back of my neck is on fire. That man suggested the library, practically herded everyone toward it, and now he's in there with her and I'm standing here holding a guest book like a fool.

The inscription on the mantelpiece — she mentioned it. A riddle. She loves riddles. Of course she does. She found a formation in a cave when she was eleven. She's brave and clever and she doesn't need me to test pens, she needs — no. She needs someone watching her back when she's too busy being brilliant to notice the danger. That's what I'm for.

The library. Now. James Hartwell does not dawdle in entrance halls while the woman he — while Miss Pitstop explores potentially dangerous rooms with a man whose smile doesn't reach his eyes. The plan is simple: get to the library, examine that inscription before anyone else can, position myself between Clara and Pemberton, and solve the riddle in a way that is both heroic and modest. Mostly heroic. Modestly heroic.

My feet are already moving. The weight has dropped into my legs — not the settling kind, the forward kind. The kind that pulled me off the bench in the schoolyard before I'd decided to stand.

events.desc: She called me 'sugar.' She calls everyone 'sugar.' It doesn't mean anything. And yet my hands are slightly unsteady. Ridiculous. Focus, Hartwell. Pemberton is already in there.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh my stars, would you look at this place! Floor-to-ceiling books — I could just live in here! And look at that mantelpiece — there's an inscription carved right into the stone. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Well, sugar, that's a riddle if I ever heard one, and Clara Bellingham does not walk away from a riddle! Now let me think... cities but no houses... forests but no trees... why, that's a map! It has to be a map! Let me take a closer look at this mantelpiece — I'll bet my best hat there's more to it than meets the eye!
events.thinking: The library. Oh, the library. The prickling at my scalp has turned into a full hum — floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, dusty leather volumes, and there it is: the carved stone mantelpiece with the inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' My fingers are warm and restless. That's a riddle, and I know this one — it's a map! A map has cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. That's the answer. But what do I do with it? The mantelpiece can be interacted with, and it says I can USE a fake-medal on it. I don't have a fake-medal. So maybe the riddle unlocks something when answered, or maybe solving it is step one and I need to find the medal elsewhere. I should interact with the mantelpiece first to see if speaking the answer does anything. Also — Dick Dastardly is here, and the Slag Brothers. Rock and Gravel. And Sneekly followed me in. I should notice — Dick Dastardly was being suspiciously polite back in the entrance hall, talking about 'historical ambiance.' Bless his heart. But I see the best in everyone, so he's just being a gentleman, isn't he? The bookshelves have several volumes that are upside down — that's peculiar. That's exactly the kind of seam that doesn't fit. But the mantelpiece riddle is pulling me harder. The pressure behind my eyes, the gravity of the unanswered thing. Let me interact with that inscription.

events.desc: A map. The answer is a map. And in a mansion hiding a legendary diamond, a map could mean everything. Those upside-down books on the shelves are nagging at me too — who shelves books upside down unless they're marking something? One mystery at a time, Clara.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the mantelpiece.

The Ant Hill Mob: There you are, Clara! Blimey, don't do that to me — one minute you're in the foyer, next minute you've vanished into a library full of — well, full of people I ain't entirely sure about, if I'm bein' honest. No offence to present company. Well — some offence, maybe. Now then, what's all this about a mantelpiece? 'Cities but no 'ouses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — sounds like one of them trick questions the coppers used to ask when they was tryin' to confuse ya. Pemberton, mate, you're very keen on that mantelpiece. Very keen indeed. What's it to ya, eh? Just wonderin'.
events.thinking: Right — there she is. Clara. In the library. Relief floods through me like warm water. She's safe. She's 'ere. But so's Pemberton, already poking at that mantelpiece like 'e knows exactly what 'e's looking for. And Dastardly's slithered in too — that's two snakes in a room with Clara, which is two more than I'm comfortable with. The Slag brothers are 'ere as well — Rock and Gravel — big lads, not the sharpest, but you never know whose side they're on in a place like this. The mantelpiece — there's a riddle on it. 'Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' That's... I dunno what that is. A map? Sounds like a map. But Pemberton's already fiddling with it, ain't 'e? Getting there first. Controlling what people find. That's what the clever ones do — they don't steal, they steer. I need to get between 'im and Clara. Physically. Just... be there. Be the wall. I'll position meself near 'er, casual like. Maybe bump into something on the way — always do — but get close. That's the job.

events.desc: Look at 'im — Pemberton — 'ands all over that stonework like 'e's searching for something specific. Not curious. Purposeful. That ain't a man solving a riddle for fun. That's a man who already knows the answer.
